title: Are these two numbers co-prime, and does one divide the other?
description: Two numbers are given only by their rows of primes. The rows are compared to see whether a prime is common, and whether one row sits inside the other.
teaching_notes: One idea: a common prime means not co-prime, and divisibility needs the whole row of the divisor inside the other row. Watch for students who think a shared prime means one divides the other.

video_script.why: The child decides co-primeness and divisibility from two rows of primes alone, the way the book compares the rows for seventy five and twenty one.
video_script.substitution: the book's own rows of primes: two times three times seven, and three times seven times eleven
video_script.anchor: two rows of primes, 2 × 3 × 7 and 3 × 7 × 11, with the common primes ringed and the others left alone
video_script.payoff_line: They are not co-prime, and neither divides the other

final_answer.value: No, they are not co-prime (3 and 7 are common). No, neither divides the other.
final_answer.spoken: they are not co-prime, and neither divides the other

maths_rules: common primes: 3 and 7, so they are not co-prime
the row of the first has a 2 that the second lacks, so the first is not inside the second
the row of the second has an 11 that the first lacks, so the second is not inside the first
check: 42 × 5 = 210 and 42 × 6 = 252, and 231 lies between, so 231 is not a multiple of 42; 42 is smaller than 231, so 42 is not a multiple of 231
video_script.design: The two rows of primes are lined up. The common primes are ringed, and the primes with no partner are left hanging.
